extracted.intended_audience: physicians, medical students, and natural philosophers (early modern learned readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A Latin early‑modern medical treatise describing human nature, anatomy, physiology, causes of longevity, diet, and disease; intended as practical and theoretical guidance for physicians and learned readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of vascular types
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of vessels in the body: surface veins that are fixed and non‑pulsating containing warm red blood, and thicker pulsating vessels (arteries) that contain the hottest, yellow blood which proceeds from the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish superficial (venous) vessels from deeper pulsating (arterial) ones; arteries arise from the heart and carry the most active (hot) blood, while superficial veins hold tepid red blood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulse as indicator of heat and bodily state
rubrics_metrics.description: The pulse (arterial motion) preserves natural heat; a strong pulse shows ardour/desire and is associated with respiration and post‑exercise sweating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pulse intensity to infer internal heat, desire, and the body's purgative movements; intense pulse indicates internal fire and forthcoming sweat; observe pulse when assessing vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiration taxonomy and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: All animals respire either openly or covertly: birds/reptiles/quadrupeds by air, fishes by gills; some aquatic animals use both air and water. Respiration frequency correlates with body size and life length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize different modes of respiration by species (gills vs lungs vs cutaneous/occult). Faster respiration tends to indicate shorter life; slow and infrequent respiration correlates with longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiration rate as sign of lifespan
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, fast‑breathing creatures tend to have brief lives; larger, slowly‑breathing creatures live longer. Slowness of respiration is a major sign of long life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging potential longevity, consider respiration frequency and growth speed: slow growth and infrequent respiration predict longer life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary causes of human longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of long life in humans is maximal internal heat (calor maximus), abundance of moist fat (humidi pinguis abundantia), and tenuity/solidity in the proper balance (tenuitas solida).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an individual's constitution for relative heat, nourishing moist fat, and appropriate tenuity of solids when estimating life span or prescribing regimens to support longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliaries that promote long life
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderate diet, abstention from excess wine, regular exercise, plentiful sleep, pure/purified air (especially easterly winds and coastal breezes), and avoidance of unnecessary bloodletting or drugs prolong life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribe moderate victuals, temperance in drink, adequate sleep and exercise, and recommend living where the air is pure and dry; avoid excessive medical interventions that cause debility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dietary elements beneficial to longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Milk (thin but sweet), oil, and honey are especially conducive to longevity; they nourish without causing gross corruption if consumed properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor easily digestible, nutritious items like milk, oil, and honey in diets aimed at long life; use fresh and well‑prepared foods and avoid overly putrid or corrupting victuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food density and life duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, denser things live longer; yet density opposed by laxity (softness) may also support long life. Thin things that cohere (do not admit fissures) can become dense and durable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess foods and bodily humours for density vs laxity: denser nutritive substances support longevity, but excessive hardness or dryness is harmful; a balance with some softness can be beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five desiderata for good bread
rubrics_metrics.description: Bread should (1) nourish well, (2) be solid as aliment, (3) be pleasant in taste, (4) not corrupt easily, and (5) be easy to procure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing or prescribing bread, ensure it satisfies all five conditions; the mode of preparation (baked by fire) is essential for palatability and preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of bread types by region and grain
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five principal kinds of bread depending on grain and region (e.g., wheat types, 'maize'/'sorgum' variants and root‑based breads), and regional differences affect their qualities and digestibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select bread appropriate to regional customs and individual constitution; note that different grains (and their processing) yield breads with different nutritive and gustatory properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of growth and augmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth occurs when cavities in a part are filled with sap/juice and expand while preserving form; increase is by nourishment adding material while the form persists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand growth as filling and consolidation of existing form rather than creation of new form; in therapy or breeding, supply nutritive material that fills and consolidates tissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of bodily substances by tenuity and density
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an ordered sequence from most tenuous to most solid: spirit (most tenuous), followed by fat, marrow, blood, phlegm, melancholy, brain, lung, flesh, liver, veins and arteries, nerves, membranes, ligaments, cartilage, and bone (most dense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this ordering to reason about vulnerability, function, and how disease or heat acts through successive substances from tenuous to solid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical principle for head/skull construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The skull must be constructed so membranes are sufficiently thin to avoid crushing the brain but bones sufficiently robust to protect against cold and injury; an excessively thick skull causes dullness and sluggish intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremes: too thin leaves brain exposed; too thick produces torpor. Observe skull thickness in prognostic and therapeutic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hair and capillary function
rubrics_metrics.description: Hair covers the head to compensate for lack of flesh and to protect; capilli are naturally thin, and hair colour/thickness correlate with heat (black hair often produced by greater heat and is thicker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider hair quality as an index of internal heat and constitution; treatments for hair loss (e.g., specific oils) should take into account the nature of the hair and underlying heat/moisture balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation: effects of mixing on offspring robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: When male and female seed mix properly (including mixing with smallest parts of the female), offspring are stronger and more robust; defective mixtures produce weak or malformed progeny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In considerations of fertility and heredity, attend to the quality and balance of generative materials; sexual practices and the states of parents influence offspring constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of venereal activity on generation and health
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent venereal usage affects temperament and generation: those engaged in long contemplation (philosophers) are less ready for love and may produce weak offspring; vice versa, frequent intercourse affects body heat and vigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise moderation: sexual habits alter disposition and reproductive outcomes; tailor counsel depending on individual's constitution and aims (e.g., vigor vs contemplative pursuits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical methods for artificial incubation
rubrics_metrics.description: Eggs require sustained warmth to produce birds; methods include use of warm cushions, artificial heat, even burying under earth or using light fire when natural brooding is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For artificial hatching, maintain even warmth and rotation until the appropriate day (noted up to ~20th day) to ensure equal incubation; avoid cooling and uneven heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and classification of contagious disease by contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Contagion via contact has four modes: contact by body (skin), by material (ulcers), by subtle vapours (affecting inner parts), and by corrupted air; different organs show corresponding diseases (skin → leprosy/scabies; lungs → ulcers; mouth/genitals → foul ulcers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose and manage contagion by identifying mode of contact and target organ; isolation and attention to the medium (air, material, direct contact) are important for prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dental deterioration causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Teeth fall in old age primarily because gums erode; chronic acidic vomiting (or acidic drinks) can corrode gums and thus cause accelerated tooth loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating dental loss or advising on oral health, consider gastric disorders (acid vomiting) and corrosive drinks as causes and address them to protect gums and teeth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humoral/contagious disease classification by site
rubrics_metrics.description: Diseases manifest according to the site of contact or corruption: skin diseases near the skin, pulmonary diseases near lungs, ulcers affect cavities and generate local symptoms, and corrupt air leads to broader putrefaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use location of symptoms to infer route and nature of contagion and to guide local vs systemic interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of excretion/separation in bodily purity
rubrics_metrics.description: Through repeated transmutations (passages through pores, membranes, and vessels) the impurer part is separated and the remaining substance becomes more tenuous and fit for tissue; insufficient separation signals poor nutrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess bodily excretions and the efficiency of separation processes (sweat, urine, feces) as indicators of nutrition and health; poor excretion suggests malnourishment or impaired renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and avoidance in food processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Foods must be properly prepared (e.g., bread baked by fire) to avoid putrefaction and to be palatable and nutritive; some regional fruits are particularly wholesome and resist putrefaction while others may be harmful if improperly prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize correct culinary technique and local food suitability; avoid raw or poorly processed foods that invite corruption or immediate harm.
